Hildegard of Bingen. A Benedictine abbess, mystic, theologian, and composer who lived from 1098 to 1179. Her liturgical chants represent the only extensive musical corpus by a woman from the medieval period, making her achievements singular in music history.

She composed approximately seventy sacred lyrics and chants, preserved in what she called the Symphonia armonie celestium revelacionum, the Symphony of the Harmony of Heavenly Revelations. These were set to flowing, emotionally direct melodies that departed from conventions of her time. She created the Ordo Virtutum, a liturgical drama pitting virtues against vice, with the human soul as protagonist. This was an early ancestor of the mystery play and music drama tradition. She founded and directed her own convent at Disibodenberg and later Rupertsberg, overseeing scriptoria, music production, and a distinguished intellectual community.

Her chants employed modal melodies with unusually large intervallic leaps and expressive contours, departing significantly from the more formulaic Gregorian tradition. Beyond music, she wrote extensively on theology, medicine, natural science, and moral philosophy. Her Liber Scivias, the Book of Divine Knowledge, detailed her mystical visions and earned papal approval during her lifetime. She claimed direct divine inspiration for both her visions and compositions, and remarkably, the Church validated this claim while she still lived. Her music embodied visionary Christian mysticism in a way that was both deeply personal and theologically rigorous.
